a: or a darkness you cannot see through
p: The Hebrew begins "or darkness"; the Greek reads "the light turned to darkness for you."

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008)
readings.en: or darkness, you will not see
readings.plain: or a darkness you cannot see through

readings.w: Septuagint (Old Greek, Rahlfs edition; checked on blueletterbible.org); adopted by Dhorme, Pope and others as reflecting Hebrew אוֹרְךָ חָשַׁךְ
readings.en: the light turned to darkness for you
readings.plain: your light has turned to darkness

why: The Hebrew is abrupt but makes sense as one more image of the dread in 22:10. The Greek may be a smoother guess or may preserve a better Hebrew text; the evidence is evenly balanced, so the Plain keeps the Masoretic Text.

p: The Hebrew says "what can the Almighty do to them"; the Greek and Syriac have "to us."

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008)
readings.en: and what can the Almighty do to them?
readings.plain: would ever do to them

readings.w: Septuagint (Old Greek, Rahlfs edition; checked on blueletterbible.org); Syriac Peshitta (as reported by Clines); most modern English versions
readings.en: what will the Almighty bring on us?
readings.plain: would ever do to us

why: The Hebrew shifts from quoted speech ("Go away from us") to reported speech ("to them"), which is natural in Hebrew poetry. The Plain makes the second line reported speech so that "them" reads naturally. The Greek and Syriac make both lines direct speech; they may be smoothing the text.

a: Still today my complaint is defiant
p: The Hebrew reads "rebellion"; the Syriac, Targum and Vulgate read "bitter."

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008)
readings.en: my complaint is rebellion
readings.plain: Still today my complaint is defiant

readings.w: Syriac Peshitta, Targum of Job, Latin Vulgate ("in amaritudine"), as reported in the commentaries; not checked directly
readings.en: my complaint is bitter
readings.plain: Still today my complaint is bitter

why: "Rebellion" is the harder reading, and scribes and translators tend to make hard readings easier. It also fits Job's refusal to soften his protest.

a: his hand lies heavy on me, though I groan
p: The Hebrew says "my hand is heavy on my groaning"; the Greek and Syriac say "his hand," and the Vulgate "the hand of my wound." The Plain follows the Greek.

readings.w: Septuagint (Old Greek, Rahlfs edition; checked on blueletterbible.org); Syriac Peshitta (as reported); most modern versions
readings.orig: ἡ χεὶρ αὐτοῦ βαρεῖα γέγονεν ἐπ᾽ ἐμῷ στεναγμῷ
readings.en: his hand has become heavy on my groaning
readings.plain: his hand lies heavy on me, though I groan

readings.w: Latin Vulgate (Clementine text, checked on sacred-texts.com)
readings.orig: manus plagæ meæ aggravata est super gemitum meum
readings.en: the hand of my wound (the blow that struck me) weighs on my groaning
readings.plain: the hand that struck me lies heavy on me, though I groan

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008)
readings.en: my hand is heavy on my groaning
readings.plain: my hand presses down on my groaning

why: "His hand" (yado) and "my hand" (yadi) differ by one stroke in Hebrew script, a common confusion. God's heavy hand is a set phrase (13:21; 33:7; Psalm 32:4), and the Greek is clear. The Masoretic Text can be explained (Job holds back his groans, or his own wound weighs on him), so its reading is shown here. The Vulgate's "hand of my wound" points the same way: the hand is the blow that falls on Job, not his own. The Old Greek's first line of the verse is quite different from the Hebrew and is not followed.

t: "More than my portion" or "in my bosom"?
p: The Hebrew says Job prized God's words above his allotted portion; the Greek says he hid them in his bosom.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008)
readings.en: more than my portion I have treasured
readings.plain: more than my own portion

readings.w: Septuagint (Old Greek, Rahlfs edition; checked on blueletterbible.org); Latin Vulgate ("in sinu meo")
readings.orig: ἐν δὲ κόλπῳ μου ἔκρυψα ῥήματα αὐτοῦ
readings.en: in my bosom I hid his words
readings.plain: in my bosom

why: The two readings differ by one letter (mem or bet). The Hebrew makes sense, since "my portion" can mean daily food (Proverbs 30:8). Many scholars prefer the Greek; the Plain stays with the Masoretic Text.

a: yet God takes no notice of the wrong
p: The Hebrew says God does not count the offense; the Syriac reads "God does not hear their prayer."

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008)
readings.en: and God does not set (regard) the offense
readings.plain: yet God takes no notice of the wrong

readings.w: Syriac Peshitta, with tefillah, "prayer" (as reported by Dhorme and Clines; not checked directly)
readings.en: and God does not hear prayer
readings.plain: yet God does not listen to their prayer

why: The Hebrew word tiflah, "what is unfitting," is rare but appears in 1:22 as well; the Syriac reading may be an easier guess. Both readings make the same charge against God.

p: The Hebrew compares the wicked man's house to a moth's; the Greek has moth and spider, the Syriac spider.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008)
readings.en: he builds his house like the moth
readings.plain: Like a moth

readings.w: Septuagint (Old Greek, Rahlfs edition; checked on blueletterbible.org) (moths and a spider); Syriac Peshitta (spider, as reported)
readings.en: like moths and like a spider
readings.plain: Like a spider

why: A moth's cocoon is a fine picture of a fragile house, and the Masoretic Text is not hard. The Greek's double image may combine two readings. The spider appears in 8:14, so a scribe could have been influenced either way.

a: but there will be no next time
p: The Plain follows the Greek and Syriac, "he will not do it again." The Hebrew reads "he will not be gathered."

readings.w: Septuagint (Old Greek, Rahlfs edition; checked on blueletterbible.org); Syriac Peshitta (as reported); most modern versions
readings.en: he will not add (do it again)
readings.plain: but there will be no next time

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); KJV
readings.en: and he will not be gathered
readings.plain: but he will not be gathered

why: The two Hebrew words are very close (yosif and ye'asef). "Not again" makes clear sense with the next line: he lies down rich, but there is no next morning for him. "Not gathered" would mean, most likely, not gathered to his fathers, that is, not given an honored burial with his ancestors (compare 2 Kings 22:20), or else that his wealth is not gathered in. It can be defended, but fits the line less well.

a: No human knows what it is worth
p: The Hebrew says no one knows wisdom's value; the Greek says no one knows its way.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008)
readings.en: a human does not know its value
readings.plain: No human knows what it is worth

readings.w: Septuagint (Old Greek, Rahlfs edition; checked on blueletterbible.org)
readings.en: a mortal does not know its way
readings.plain: No human knows the way to it

why: The Greek matches 28:23 ("God grasps the way to it") and the poem's theme of where wisdom is, and many scholars adopt it. But "its value" prepares for the list of prices in 28:15–19, and it is the harder reading. The Plain keeps the Masoretic Text.

a: and I will make my days as many as the sand
p: The Hebrew chol is "sand"; rabbinic tradition read "phoenix"; the Greek has "the trunk of a palm tree."

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008) (most translations)
readings.en: and like the sand I will multiply days
readings.plain: and I will make my days as many as the sand

readings.w: Rabbinic tradition (Genesis Rabbah 19:5; Talmud Sanhedrin 108b): chol as the phoenix
readings.en: like the phoenix I will multiply days
readings.plain: and like the phoenix I will make my days many

readings.w: Septuagint (Old Greek, Rahlfs edition; checked on blueletterbible.org)
readings.orig: ὥσπερ στέλεχος φοίνικος πολὺν χρόνον βιώσω
readings.en: like the trunk of a palm tree I will live a long time
readings.plain: and like the trunk of a palm tree I will live a long time

why: "Sand" is the plain meaning of the word and a common picture of countless numbers. The phoenix reading fits "die in my nest" and has old support; the Greek's word phoinix (palm, also phoenix) may reflect the same tradition. The Plain keeps the common reading.

p: Both readings belong to the Masoretic Text: the written consonants (Ketiv) say "his cord," the reading tradition (Qere) "my cord."

readings.w: Qere (the Masoretic reading tradition, Leningrad Codex vowels)
readings.en: he has loosened my cord (bowstring or tent cord)
readings.plain: He has slackened my cord

readings.w: Ketiv (the written consonants of the Masoretic Text)
readings.en: he has loosened his cord
readings.plain: He has slackened his cord

why: With "my cord," God has slackened Job's bowstring or the cord of his tent, taking away his strength (contrast 29:20; 4:21). With "his cord," the verb is still singular: God has loosened his own restraint on Job, or the mob, taken as one body, has thrown off its restraint, as in the next line. The Plain follows the Qere, which is the Masoretic reading, so this is not a departure from the Masoretic Text.

a: With great force my clothes are pulled out of shape
p: The Hebrew says Job's garment is disfigured; the Greek says God seized his robe.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008)
readings.en: by great force my garment disguises itself
readings.plain: With great force my clothes are pulled out of shape

readings.w: Septuagint (Old Greek, Rahlfs edition; checked on blueletterbible.org); followed by many modern versions
readings.orig: ἐν πολλῇ ἰσχύι ἐπελάβετό μου τῆς στολῆς
readings.en: with great strength he took hold of my robe
readings.plain: With great force he grabs hold of my clothes

why: The Hebrew is strange but can describe a body so wasted or swollen that the clothes no longer fit. The Greek gives an easier sense and fits 30:19, where God throws Job into the mud. The Plain keeps the Masoretic Text and shows the Greek.

t: You look, or you do not look?
p: Most Hebrew manuscripts say God "looks at" Job; one manuscript and the Vulgate add "not."

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008)
readings.en: and you consider me
readings.plain: you just look me over

readings.w: One Hebrew manuscript (as reported in BHS); Latin Vulgate ("et non respicis me"); KJV supplies "not"
readings.en: and you do not consider me
readings.plain: you do not even look at me

why: The negative looks like a copy of the first line's "not." Without it the line is harsher: God watches and does nothing. The Masoretic Text has the stronger support.

a: you dissolve me in the crashing storm
t: The crash of the storm or my success?
p: The written consonants suggest "crash, roar"; the reading tradition reads "success."

readings.w: Ketiv (written consonants) read as teshu'ah, "crash" (as in 36:29); most modern versions
readings.en: you melt me in the crash
readings.plain: you dissolve me in the crashing storm

readings.w: Qere (Masoretic reading tradition); KJV "dissolvest my substance"
readings.en: you melt away (my) success
readings.plain: you dissolve all my success

why: The storm image runs through the verse, and teshu'ah means the crash of a storm in 36:29. The Qere's "success" is possible but leaves the verb without a natural object.

a: Surely, from the rubble, a man stretches out his hand
t: A cry for help or a wish to die?
p: The Hebrew is obscure. The Greek turns the verse into Job's wish that he could take his own life.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008) (as most modern scholars read it)
readings.en: surely in a ruin one stretches out a hand
readings.plain: Surely, from the rubble, a man stretches out his hand

readings.w: Septuagint (Old Greek, Rahlfs edition; checked on blueletterbible.org)
readings.orig: εἰ γὰρ ὄφελον δυναίμην ἐμαυτὸν χειρώσασθαι ἢ δεηθείς γε ἑτέρου καὶ ποιήσει μοι τοῦτο
readings.en: if only I could lay hands on myself, or ask another, and he would do this for me
readings.plain: If only I could lay hands on myself, or ask another to do it for me!

why: The Greek translator seems to have read the Hebrew differently or guessed at it. The Hebrew, though hard, fits the context of a cry for help (30:20, 28).

a: if I have hidden my wrongs as Adam did
p: The Hebrew has "like Adam" (or "as people do"); the Greek reads "if I sinned unwillingly and hid my sin."

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008)
readings.en: if I covered like Adam (or: like humans) my transgressions
readings.plain: if I have hidden my wrongs as Adam did

readings.w: Septuagint (Old Greek, Rahlfs edition; checked on blueletterbible.org)
readings.orig: εἰ δὲ καὶ ἁμαρτὼν ἀκουσίως ἔκρυψα τὴν ἁμαρτίαν μου
readings.en: if, having sinned unwillingly, I hid my sin
readings.plain: if I sinned without meaning to and hid my sin

why: The Greek seems to paraphrase. The Hebrew ke'adam is clear in its letters; the debate is only whether it means Adam or people in general (see the note).

a: those who rose against us are wiped out
p: The Hebrew says "our adversaries" are destroyed; the Greek says "their substance has vanished."

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008)
readings.en: surely our adversary is destroyed
readings.plain: those who rose against us are wiped out

readings.w: Septuagint (Old Greek, Rahlfs edition; checked on blueletterbible.org); adopted by Dhorme and others as reflecting Hebrew קִימָם, "their substance"
readings.orig: εἰ μὴ ἠφανίσθη ἡ ὑπόστασις αὐτῶν
readings.en: has not their substance vanished?
readings.plain: all they owned is wiped out

why: The Hebrew qimanu, "those who rise against us," is a rare word but makes sense on the lips of the righteous who watch the wicked fall (22:19). The Greek gives a smoother parallel with the second line ("what they had to spare"), which may be why it was chosen. The Plain keeps the Masoretic Text.

a: and like everyone they shrink away
p: The Hebrew says the wicked shrink away "like all"; the Greek says they wither "like mallow in the heat."

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008)
readings.en: like all (others) they are shut up (shrink away)
readings.plain: and like everyone they shrink away

readings.w: Septuagint (Old Greek, Rahlfs edition; checked on blueletterbible.org) ("like mallow in the heat"), reflecting Hebrew כַּמַּלּוּחַ; adopted by many modern scholars
readings.en: like mallow in the heat
readings.plain: and like mallow they shrink away

why: The Greek fits the plant picture of the next line (heads of grain) and the same plant name appears in 30:4, so many scholars adopt it. But "like everyone" makes good sense in Job's mouth: the wicked do die, but no differently from anyone else (21:23–26). The Plain keeps the Masoretic Text.

p: The Hebrew says "there is no helper for them"; many moderns change one letter to read "no one restrains them."

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008)
readings.en: there is no helper for them
readings.plain: they need nobody's help

readings.w: Modern conjecture, Hebrew עֹצֵר ('otser, "one who restrains") for עֹזֵר ('ozer); RSV, ESV and others. No manuscript or ancient version has it.
readings.en: there is no one to restrain them
readings.plain: no one holds them back

why: The Masoretic Text can mean that the mob needs no one's help to ruin Job, or that no one helps Job against them. The conjecture gives an easier line, but it has no support in any witness, so the Plain keeps the Masoretic Text.
